scenes.title: RANK()
scenes.narration: RANK assigns a ranking position within a partition where tied rows share the same rank and the next rank skips ahead, leaving gaps.

scenes.title: How RANK() Behaves
bullets: Rows are ranked by the ORDER BY inside OVER
Tied rows receive the same rank
The next rank skips, creating gaps (1, 1, 3)
scenes.narration: RANK orders rows by the ORDER BY clause and assigns a position to each. When rows tie they share the same rank. Critically, the next distinct value skips ahead by the number of tied rows, so you get sequences like one, one, three. As with all window functions, ranking restarts when a new partition begins.

scenes.title: Ranking Exam Scores
scenes.code:
SELECT
  student,
  score,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rnk
FROM exam_results;
scenes.narration: This query ranks students by their exam score from highest to lowest. If two students both score ninety-five, they each receive rank one. The very next student, no matter their score, receives rank three rather than two, because the tie consumed the second position. That skipped number is the hallmark gap that RANK produces.

scenes.title: What Happens on a Tie
steps: Two rows share the highest value → both get rank 1
One rank position is consumed by the tie
The next value gets rank 3, not 2
The gap reflects how many rows came before it
scenes.narration: When a tie occurs, both rows take the same rank and effectively consume the positions between them. The following row's rank equals the count of rows that came before it plus one. That is why after two rows tied at rank one, the next row jumps to rank three, leaving a visible gap at position two.

scenes.text: Choose RANK() when gaps are meaningful — like leaderboards or competition standings where two people sharing 1st place means there is genuinely no 2nd place.
scenes.narration: Use RANK when the gap after a tie carries real meaning, such as competition standings where a shared first place truly means there is no second place.
